speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: I grew up in a family where I was told I could be anything that I wanted to be and sadly it wasn't until I got into the military that I realized there were restrictions on me just because I was a woman and so it just really torqued me off and I decided I was going to be a fighter pilot just because they told me that I couldn't you I'm Congresswoman Martha McSally. I was the first woman to actually fly in combat in U.S. history and then later on to command a fighter squadron in combat. I remember that first trip. It was a couple hours in the middle of the night from one base to another and my subordinates I was the highest ranking person in the car and they're all wearing jeans or khakis and polo shirts and I'm sitting there in this traditional garb which is the Abaya and Abaya Headscarf. I mean think about that. I can fly a single seat attack aircraft into enemy territory but I can't drive. and I'm told to sit in the back seat of a car, and then always be accompanied by a man. I mean, women in Saudi Arabia don't have the same rights as men, so this policy was dysfunctional on so many levels. It was bad for good order and discipline, and it was really sacrificing America's values as we were serving overseas. We were the uniform to protect religious freedoms. When we raise our right hand and we take an oath as a military officer, it's to support and defend the constitution of the United States against all enemies foreign and domestic. We thought originally it was something that the Saudis were imposing. or the State Department, and in my research I discovered that it was just a not well thought out Pentagon imposed policy. A little did I know I would start an eight year journey of researching where this policy came from and shepherded some legislation that finally overturned the ridiculous policy once and for all. The whole thing was an eight year battle. I call myself a feminist Republican and I don't believe that's an oxymoron. I believe that the values that we have in the Republican Party and what we were founded on are good for men and women in our country. I've been fighting stereotypes my whole life. I don't group men and women into categories and make stereotypes about them. But we need to recognize that I think women still have untapped potential in America, that even though we've removed most of the structural barriers, we still have some cultural barriers, and those are very real to women and young girls. And if you really believe in equal opportunity, then you need to believe in that, and you need to let women and girls be whatever it is they want to be, not what you think they should be. But if you believe that you want to have the opportunity to compete and to be able to succeed and do whatever it is that you have the potential to do, where the playing field is leveled and then you have that opportunity, then that's where I would hope we could be able to attract more women and the values of feminism really to better line up with what we believe as Republicans. We should pick the best man for the job, even if she's a woman. And that's what America is all about. And I believe that's what really my view of feminism is.

explicit_propositions.text: I was raised in a family that encouraged me to pursue any career I desired.
I initially believed I could achieve any goal regardless of gender.
I discovered gender-based restrictions in the military after joining.
The restriction I encountered was due solely to my being a woman.
My reaction to the restriction was anger and frustration.
I chose to become a fighter pilot specifically because I was told I couldn't.

assumptions.text: Gender should not limit personal ambition or professional aspirations.
Personal determination can overcome institutional resistance.
Being denied opportunities based on gender undermines individual dignity.
Rejection of a limitation motivates stronger commitment to prove oneself.
There is moral value in defying unjust policies.
Self-determination is central to authentic achievement.
